title: Babylon Arrives: The First Exile from Jerusalem
summary: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon makes Jehoiakim his vassal, and when Jehoiakim rebels, raiders from several nations are sent against Judah, which the narrator explains as the LORD's judgment for Manasseh's sins. Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin reigns three months before Jerusalem is besieged and he surrenders. Nebuchadnezzar carries off the king, the royal family, the leading men, the soldiers, and the craftsmen, strips the temple's gold, and installs Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as king under the name Zedekiah, who in turn rebels.
story: Chapter 23 ended with Judah under Egyptian control after Josiah's death. Now the power that Isaiah had named to Hezekiah in 20:17 arrives, and its first blows land. This chapter tells of the first of two great deportations from Jerusalem. The narrator is careful to explain it theologically before describing it: this happened at the LORD's command (verse 3), because of Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood he shed. The treasures of the temple and palace go to Babylon, just as Isaiah warned. The chapter ends with Zedekiah's rebellion, setting up the final siege and destruction in chapter 25. For the book's first readers, many of them exiles themselves, this chapter named the beginning of their own story.
historical:
The shift of power happened quickly. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, then crown prince of Babylon, defeated Pharaoh Neco at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Egypt lost its hold on Syria and Palestine; verse 7 summarizes the result. Nebuchadnezzar became king the same year and ruled until 562 BC. Jehoiakim submitted, then rebelled, probably after Babylon and Egypt fought an indecisive battle near Egypt's border around 601 BC, which the Babylonian Chronicle records. Before the Babylonian army could return in force, raiders from surrounding peoples harassed Judah (verse 2).

Jehoiakim died in late 598 BC, and his eighteen-year-old son Jehoiachin inherited the siege. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar captured the city of Judah in the month of Adar in his seventh year, which corresponds to March 597 BC, seized its king, and appointed a king of his own choosing, which matches this chapter closely. (The chapter counts the event as Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year, which may reflect a different way of reckoning the year.) The prophet Ezekiel was among the exiles of 597 and dates his visions by the years of Jehoiachin's exile (Ezekiel 1:2). Jeremiah stayed in Jerusalem and wrote to the exiles, telling them to settle in Babylon and seek its welfare (Jeremiah 29). Zedekiah reigned from 597 to 586 BC.
cultural:
Babylon, like Assyria before it, dealt with rebellious vassals by removing the people most capable of leading a revolt: the royal family, officials, soldiers, and skilled workers. Craftsmen and metalsmiths were especially valuable, both because they could make weapons and because the empire needed skilled labor for its building projects. Leaving only the poorest people of the land (verse 14) kept the territory farmed and taxed but powerless.

Changing a vassal king's name, as Nebuchadnezzar did with Mattaniah and as Neco had done with Eliakim (23:34), was a sign of the overlord's authority. The new name Zedekiah means the LORD is righteous, an irony the book's readers would not miss, since his reign ended the kingdom. The queen mother (verses 12 and 15) held real influence in Judah's court, which is why the mothers of Judah's kings are named throughout Kings and why she is listed among the captives. Jeremiah 22:24-30 and 13:18 speak of Jehoiachin (called Coniah) and his mother going into exile.
literary: The chapter is built from three regnal accounts, each shorter and more compressed than the last, as the kingdom's end approaches. The Jehoiakim section (verses 1-7) stops for an unusually direct theological statement in verses 2-4, repeating the words "the LORD" and "according to the word" to insist that Babylon's arrival is the fulfillment of prophecy, not an accident of history. The Jehoiachin section (verses 8-17) is the longest and uses the vocabulary of exile: carried into exile, captives, carried away. Lists of who was taken pile up in verses 14-16, emphasizing how much was lost. The Zedekiah section (verses 18-20) begins a new account that runs into chapter 25, and its last sentence, about Zedekiah's rebellion, is left hanging.

outline.t: Jehoiakim's rebellion and the LORD's judgment
Treasures and people carried to Babylon
Zedekiah made king, and his rebellion

doctrines.note: The chapter insists that Babylon's success was the LORD's command. God's judgment works through the rise and fall of empires, and what looks like a political disaster is described as the fulfillment of his word.

Nebuchadnezzar acts for his own reasons, yet verse 2 says the LORD sent the raiders and verse 13 says the temple was stripped as the LORD had declared. God rules over the plans of the most powerful kings.
Verses 3-4 name the innocent blood Manasseh shed as a sin the LORD would not pardon. Sin has consequences that outlast the sinner, and a society that sheds innocent blood brings judgment on itself.

words.note: Salach, to forgive or pardon. In the Old Testament only God is ever the subject of this verb; people forgive, but this word is reserved for divine pardon. Verse 4 says the LORD was unwilling to forgive, one of the starkest statements in the book. The word appears in Solomon's temple prayer, which asked God to hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:30); here that prayer meets its limit.

Golah, exile or the body of exiles. It comes from the verb galah, to uncover or go into exile, and came to be used for the community of Judeans in Babylon. The word marks a new stage in the story of God's people: from here on, much of the Old Testament is written from or about the golah.

Marad, to rebel. Both Jehoiakim (verse 1) and Zedekiah (verse 20) rebel against Babylon. The prophets, especially Jeremiah, urged submission to Babylon as God's judgment, so rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar was in effect resistance to God's word. The same verb was used of Hezekiah's rebellion against Assyria (18:7), which the LORD blessed; the difference was whether the king was acting in faith or in defiance of the prophets.

christ: The chapter contains a thread that runs straight to Jesus. Jehoiachin, the king carried off in 597, was the last king of Judah in the direct line of David to reign by inheritance, and Jeremiah said none of his offspring would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Yet Jehoiachin, under the name Jechoniah, appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:11-12), in the line through which the promise to David passed during the exile. The royal line did not die in Babylon. The last chapter of Kings will return to Jehoiachin, still alive in exile, a sign that God had not finished with David's house. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David who took up that interrupted line, and whose kingdom did not depend on the thrones of Jerusalem or Babylon.

hard.q: What does it mean that the LORD was unwilling to forgive?
hard.a:
Verse 4 is hard to read alongside the many passages that celebrate God's readiness to forgive. It does not mean that no individual in Judah could be forgiven; Jeremiah and Ezekiel, prophesying at this time, call individuals to repent and promise mercy to those who do. What the LORD would not pardon was the nation's accumulated guilt, in the sense of cancelling the judgment on Jerusalem as a political and religious community. That judgment had been announced and deferred for generations, and even Josiah's reform had not turned the people's hearts for good.

The prophets also make clear that judgment was not God's last word. Jeremiah, while announcing that the exile could not be avoided, promised a return after seventy years and a new covenant in which God would forgive iniquity and remember sin no more (Jeremiah 29:10; 31:34). The refusal to forgive in verse 4 concerns the verdict on Jerusalem, not the limits of God's mercy toward those who turn to him.

questions: The narrator explains the exile before describing it. Why might it matter to see painful events through God's purposes and not only through politics?
The Babylonians took the leaders, the soldiers, and the craftsmen, and left the poor. What does a community lose when its skilled and capable people are taken away, and what might remain?
Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they were sent. How might that counsel shape the way Christians live in places that are not their true home?
